congressionalglo7395unit:741:par_000741_.text: He cannot give a license or indulgence to com- mit crime ; but after a crime is committed, all he has to do in his certificate is to specify par- ticularly the crime that has been committed and for which the pardon is granted. But it may well be denied that but for the act of Con- gress of July 17, 1862, of which my friend from New Hampshire before me [Mr. CLARK] was perhaps the chief draughtsman, the President would have any authority to grant a general pardon or amnesty. I must admit that act is quite full. Let me refer to it. The thirteenth section is in these words :

"SEC. 13. And be it further enacted, That the Presi- dent is hereby authorized, at any time hereafter, by proclamation, to extend to persons who may have participated in the existing rebellion in any State or part thereof, pardon and amnesty, with such excep- tions and at such time and on such conditions as he may deem expedient for the public welfare."

It will not be disputed that by virtue of that authority the President had power to issue his proclamation of general amnesty. But disputes may arise on other questions connected with this proclamation. What was the condition upon which the pardon was to inure to the benefit of the party pardoned? It was first that he should file the oath named and in the manner to be prescribed. But this is not of itself sufficient. There is something more necessary that the benefits of the pardon should inure.
